title: How to lead a design interview
summary: Use the hour to make decisions, test assumptions and invite useful disagreement.

steps.title: The prompt is only five words
steps.text: You are asked to design a notification service. You could spend the hour drawing queues, but nobody has said whether messages are promotional emails or urgent medical alerts. Leading the discussion starts by turning a vague noun into a user journey and a few testable promises. State a provisional scope and ask which assumption would most change the design.

steps.title: A flexible plan for sixty minutes
steps.text: Use roughly 0 to 8 minutes for users, scope, exclusions and failure promises. Spend 8 to 15 on traffic, payload and storage estimates. Use 15 to 30 to draw one complete request path and explain the data model. Spend 30 to 47 on the hardest constraint: a hot key, a partial failure, consistency or recovery. Use 47 to 55 to test failures, cost and operations, and leave 55 to 60 to summarize decisions and open questions. These are checkpoints, not a script. If a requirement reveals a major risk, move the depth earlier and say why.

steps.title: Worked example: choose the deep question
steps.text: Assume 10 million users receive 3 notifications/day. That is 30 million/day, or about 347/s average. With a 10 times burst, plan about 3,470/s. At an assumed 1 KB payload, raw events add about 30 GB/day, before replicas and delivery attempts. If the provider admits only 2,000/s, an extra app fleet cannot erase the downstream limit. A five-minute 3,470/s burst creates about 441,000 queued notifications if service stays at 2,000/s. That calculation suggests going deep on admission, deadlines and recovery. It is a worked design exercise, not a sim run.

steps.q: Eight minutes in, nobody knows if delivery can wait. What should you do?
choices: State the ambiguity and agree a deadline before choosing the queue policy
steps.why: The delivery deadline changes buffering, cost and failure behavior.

steps.q: Why did you spend time on numbers before choosing services? Follow-up: your traffic estimate is wrong by ten times.
checklist: Connect estimates to bottlenecks and guarantees
Show sensitivity rather than false precision
Keep the scope and unknowns explicit
steps.model: The estimates tell us whether a single store, provider or network path is plausible. I would mark them as assumptions and test a tenfold range. If the provider is already the bottleneck at the lower end, the core design needs admission and buffering regardless of extra app servers. If only the upper end requires partitioning, I can present a simple first design and a measured trigger for changing it. Numbers guide decisions; they are not a claim to know future traffic exactly.

steps.title: Make the reasoning visible
steps.text: Say which numbers are assumptions and which would come from measurement. Explain one simple design before alternatives. Tie each component to a requirement and name what happens on failure. Ask for pushback on a concrete decision: is delayed delivery acceptable for this message class? If you do not know a provider limit, give a plausible range, show how the design changes across it and name the measurement needed. Do not invent certainty. End with the key invariant, the bottleneck, the cost driver and one unresolved risk. A good discussion can disagree with your choice because it can see why you made it.

steps.q: The provider limit is unknown. Which response is strongest?
choices: Assert a precise number without evidence
State a range, derive sensitivity and say what to measure
steps.why: A transparent assumption lets the discussion test whether it changes the architecture.

steps.q: I disagree with your choice of deep dive. How do you respond? Follow-up: there are only fifteen minutes left.
checklist: Restate the requirement the choice serves
Reallocate time and close with decisions
steps.model: I would explain the risk I was trying to resolve and ask which requirement the alternative threatens more. If the concern changes the design, I would shift the remaining time and state what will stay at a high level. I would leave a few minutes to summarize the invariant, the chosen path and unresolved questions. The goal is a shared, defensible decision, not defending my original agenda at any cost.

steps.q: You have ten minutes left and four unexplored topics. What leads the design?
choices: Choose the highest-risk constraint, test it and summarize the remaining risks
Rush through every component at equal depth
Start over with a larger architecture
steps.why: Depth should follow the requirement most likely to invalidate the design.

takeaway: Lead with a user promise, make assumptions testable and spend depth where it can change the design.
